The 11.9% walk rate pairs with an 18.7% strikeout rate, a combination that keeps the .358 OBP credible rather than lucky. The profile hinges on zone management, because the chase and whiff numbers sit in the dead middle of the league and pitchers will probe that as he becomes a known commodity. If the discipline holds, you're looking at a perennial Silver Slugger candidate; if it softens, the raw power still plays but the OBP erodes and the .891 OPS gets trimmed.

reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The .359 xwOBA and 49.0% hard-hit rate sit in the top tier of contact quality, but a 27.0% strikeout rate and 34.1% chase rate are the friction points keeping the floor honest. The xBA landing at .251 is what that looks like in practice: power that translates, average that doesn't fully follow. What makes the profile work anyway is the 11.9% walk rate pulling the OBP toward .367 in the projection, and 29.5 ft/s sprint speed that turns baserunning into a separate weapon, projecting to 38 stolen bases alongside 37 home runs. If he ever tightens the zone discipline enough to shave the chase rate, the xwOBA already says the power is pointed at something big; if he doesn't, this is still a very useful player, just one who runs a high-variance at-bat until further notice.

reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The .409 xwOBA and 2.72 xERA exist in the same Statcast card, for the same human being. As a hitter, the contact quality is genuine: 93.5 mph average exit velocity, a 16.7% barrel rate, and a 13.1% walk rate that more than compensates for a 23.1% strikeout rate that looks scarier than it plays. reports.name: Sal Stewart
reports.published_report: Thirty-three projected home runs with a 13.3% barrel rate tells you the power shape is legitimate, even if the 38.6% hard-hit rate says he's getting there by squaring the ball perfectly rather than mashing everything in the zone. The xSLG sits at .474 and the xwOBA at .348, both well above the contact numbers suggest at first glance, because his damage when he connects is disproportionate to his raw exit velocity. The 27.0% whiff rate is the thing to watch: it's not disqualifying at 21.9% strikeouts, but if pitchers learn to exploit it and the rate climbs, the gap between his expected and actual production narrows fast. At 22, the floor here is a legitimate middle-of-the-order corner bat; the ceiling is something considerably more dangerous if the hit tool grows into the power.

reports.name: CJ Abrams
reports.published_report: Thirty-five home runs and 30 steals from a shortstop is a rare combination, and the Statcast profile explains how it's happening without being a pure contact story. The power reads as legitimate at a 10.3% barrel rate with an .xSLG of .446, even though the 89.5 mph average exit velocity is right at the median, because he's generating barrels efficiently rather than just mashing everything hard. What makes him genuinely dangerous is that the projection's .273/.347/.511 line assumes his legs keep doing real work alongside the pop, and at 28.5 ft/s he has the speed to post 30 steals in a full season. The catch in the profile is the 37.2% chase rate, which is a real liability, and if pitchers learn to exploit it more aggressively the strikeouts climb past 23.2% and the walks stay stuck near 8.6%, which puts pressure on everything downstream.

His 90.8 mph average exit velocity grades well, his 10.2% walk rate is solid, and the 40 projected stolen bases keep him relevant in the run-scoring picture even if the .219 projection looks ugly on the back of a baseball card. But a 31.4% whiff rate undercuts all of it, and the .209 xBA is the number that tells you why: he's making too little contact on pitches he swings at for the exit-velocity profile to matter at scale. Paredes makes contact at an elite clip, but 86.1 mph average exit velocity and a 28.6% hard-hit rate say the contact isn't doing enough damage, which is why the xSLG sits at .378 despite a projected .429 SLG. The profile hinges on whether that gap closes, because if pitchers keep attacking him and he keeps putting the ball in play softly, 22 projected home runs starts to look generous. He's a useful regular, but a 9.6% walk rate and the strikeout avoidance are carrying more weight than they should in a corner-infield bat.

reports.name: Ozzie Albies
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is almost entirely bottom-third contact quality: 86.9 mph average exit velocity, a 4.3% barrel rate, 28.2% hard-hit, and yet the projection still gets to 25 home runs across 685 plate appearances. That gap is the whole tension here. Albies runs a 14.1% strikeout rate that most hitters with this much swing-and-miss in the zone could never sustain, and his ability to put the ball in play at volume is what converts soft contact into counting stats. The .285 xwOBA tells you what the underlying batted-ball profile actually earns, and the .308 OBP is where the projection lands when you blend that with a walk rate sitting below league average, leaving him as a second-division regular whose power number is a product of volume, not damage.

reports.name: Michael Busch
reports.published_report: The walk rate is doing a lot of work here. At 12.4%, Busch draws free passes at a rate that puts him well into the top quartile of the league, and it's what inflates an otherwise middling contact profile into a .347 OBP, which is the number that matters most for his value case. The xBA sits at .234 and the 88.1 mph average exit velocity doesn't suggest a guy who's going to outrun his strikeouts with hard contact, so the ceiling is essentially what the projection says it is: 20 home runs, a useful OBP, a .744 OPS across a full 704 PA season. If the zone discipline erodes, the contact floor has nowhere to hide.

reports.name: Eury Pérez
reports.published_report: 172 strikeouts projected across 156.9 innings with a 3.37 ERA is a tidy front-of-rotation line for a 23-year-old, and the Statcast profile mostly backs the optimism. The fastball sits at 98.3 mph with 2677 rpm of spin, which is the engine behind a 26.9 K% and a 28.6 whiff rate that both grade well into the top quarter of starters. The tension in the profile is the walk rate: 9.9 BB% is a genuine liability, the one number that separates a near-ace ceiling from a frustrating mid-rotation reality, and the 9.2 barrel rate says hitters are squaring him up more often than those strikeout numbers suggest they should. If the command sharpens even modestly, the stuff plays up; if it doesn't, the walks and barrels coexist in a way that keeps the xERA at 3.65 and the ceiling capped.

reports.name: Cristopher Sánchez
reports.published_report: The chase rate is where the conversation starts: 36.9% gets into the 96th percentile among starters, and a 32.8% whiff rate follows from it like a necessary conclusion. Hitters can't lay off, and when they swing, they miss. The walk rate at 5.6% is exceptional control for a staff ace, which is effectively what ValuCast sees when it runs a 2.58 ERA projection over 203.3 innings — but the Statcast contact profile tells a more complicated story, because the 41.8% hard-hit rate sits in the bottom quarter of the league, meaning when he does get hit, it tends to hurt. reports.name: Mason Miller
reports.published_report: A 47.0% whiff rate and a .188 xwOBA tell you what Miller actually is: a reliever hitters can barely make contact with, and when they do, the ball doesn't go anywhere hard. His 101.5 mph fastball with 2530 rpm of spin explains why the swing-and-miss numbers hold — that's not a profile that gifts contact. The one crack in the wall is a 9.5% walk rate, which sits well below the elite tier of his other metrics, and if that number creeps up it's the only real lever opposing offenses have. Everything else projects to a 1.15 ERA and 38 saves across a full season, and there's nothing in the Statcast profile that argues against believing it.

The 98.1 mph fastball and a 33.4% chase rate explain the strikeouts; the 8.0% walk rate is the one thing keeping this from being a genuinely elite reliever profile rather than just a very good one. reports.name: Cade Smith
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is elite and the contact allowed is a genuine concern, and those two facts live in the same profile without resolving each other. Smith sits at 34.2% K rate and a 34.5% whiff rate, both comfortably in the top few percent of relievers, yet hitters are barreling him up at 9.0% and making hard contact at 46.6%, which together explain why his xERA lands at 3.15 even as the raw ERA has been well below that. The 97.4 mph fastball is doing the strikeout work, and the walk rate at 8.5% isn't a disqualifier, but the whole profile hinges on whether the swing-and-miss stays loud enough to keep that hard contact from mattering. If the whiff rate holds, he's a legitimate high-leverage closer; if it erodes, the exit velocity numbers have nowhere to hide.

reports.name: James Tibbs III
reports.published_report: The .417 OBP and 85 walks at AAA in 523 plate appearances are the load-bearing numbers here, and the MLB translation keeps the story intact: a 13.2% walk rate where the AAA average sits at 8.5%, with an ISO that translates to .19. Tibbs is a 23-year-old first baseman who has essentially answered the discipline question, and the power is enough to matter rather than just profile. The catch is position: a first baseman lives or dies by whether that bat fully arrives in MLB conditions, and the translated strikeout rate at 23.6% where MLB average runs 22.0% means the zone control that looks clean at AAA gets stress-tested at the next level. If the walk rate holds and the strikeouts don't spike, he's a low-end everyday regular; if the contact erodes under better stuff, there's a bench bat underneath it all.

Perdomo's 12.4% strikeout rate and 14.1% walk rate are both top-tier, the kind of zone command that usually drags slugging along with it, but a 3.1% barrel rate and 87.4 mph average exit velocity say the bat-to-ball skill shows up in the walk and strikeout columns while the damage stays modest. The projection (.357 OBP, .378 SLG) reflects exactly that split: a hitter who reaches base at a strong clip, steals 22 bases, and contributes without ever scaring a pitcher into a mistake. If the exit velocity creeps up even modestly, he becomes a well-rounded everyday shortstop; if it doesn't, he's a high-OBP, low-slug regular whose value lives entirely in the counting categories the power can't touch.

reports.name: Jeremy Peña
reports.published_report: The gap between his .280 xBA (89th percentile) and the raw contact quality underneath it tells the story here: Peña makes contact at an elite rate given how little he actually punishes the ball, with an average exit velocity of 88.3 mph and a 5.3% barrel rate that rank in the bottom quarter of the league. The 36.7% chase rate is the real ceiling question: if pitchers continue to exploit it, the walk rate at 6.2% won't budge, and the profile slims from a solid everyday shortstop into a bat-last regular who leans entirely on speed and placement to stay viable.

reports.name: Riley Greene
reports.published_report: A 14.6% barrel rate with a 12.4% walk rate is a legitimately dangerous offensive profile, and the .363 xwOBA says the underlying quality of contact is well ahead of what his actual slash has shown Detroit fans. The tension in Greene's profile is straightforward: he barrels the ball at a rate that puts him in genuine company, he draws walks, he doesn't chase at an alarming rate, but 27.0% strikeouts bleed enough value that his xBA sits at .258 even when his xSLG is .478. If that strikeout rate drifts lower, the power and patience combination cashes into something approaching a true middle-of-the-order bat. At its current level, he's a .269/.359/.452 producer, a very good everyday outfielder who leaves real production in the batter's box.

reports.name: Seth Hernandez
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is the loudest thing on the page, and the walk rate is the thing you have to watch. Across A+ & A in 2026, Seth Hernandez has struck out 118 batters in 74 innings, 14.3 per nine, with a K-BB% of 30 that sits in the 99th percentile of his pool, and a 2.4 ERA with a 1.1 WHIP. Translated to a major-league context, that strikeout rate softens to something around league average, and the walk rate, 3.8 per nine in the minors translating to 4.0, is the honest ceiling tax: if the command doesn't sharpen, the swing-and-miss isn't enough to carry a rotation spot. Back-end starter if it comes together; depth arm if it doesn't.

reports.name: Nico Hoerner
reports.published_report: The xBA at the 100th percentile tells you exactly who he is: a hitter who makes more contact than almost anyone alive, just without the thump to weaponize it. A 1.1% barrel rate and 85.9 mph average exit velocity sit near the bottom of the league, which is why a .301 xBA translates to a .376 xSLG and nine projected home runs across 686 plate appearances. What keeps the profile honest is the 8.6% strikeout rate, one of the cleanest in the sport, paired with 25 projected steals, so the value lives in volume and baserunning rather than damage. Everything hinges on that contact quality holding — if the bat-to-ball edge ever softens, there's not enough power underneath to carry him, and he becomes a utility piece rather than an everyday middle infielder.

reports.name: Spencer Torkelson
reports.published_report: The tension in Torkelson's Statcast card is almost comical: a 12.8% barrel rate sitting at the 86th percentile, paired with a 31.0% strikeout rate at the 7th. He makes elite contact when he makes contact, and then misses an enormous amount, which is why that .218 xBA lands at the 8th percentile while his .405 xSLG is roughly average. The 22.3% chase rate at the 90th percentile tells you the discipline is genuine, so the strikeout problem isn't a zone-recognition failure — it's a whiff rate of 31.3% on pitches he swings at, meaning pitchers who can exploit that in-zone weakness will keep him from translating the barrel quality into an average worth tolerating. If the contact rate firms up even modestly, there's a solid middle-of-the-order piece here; if it doesn't, the projection's .223/.313/.411 line is a reasonable ceiling for a first baseman who strikes out nearly a third of the time.

The projection's .772 OPS on 467 PA feels honest given what the exit-velo and hard-hit numbers say: not a soft-contact hitter, not a loud one either, just a guy in the dead middle of the contact-quality spectrum. reports.name: Munetaka Murakami
reports.published_report:
The Statcast contact profile is genuinely alarming: a 42.2% whiff rate and 32.8% strikeout rate near the bottom of the league, sitting next to a chase rate of just 22.0% that ranks elite. He sees the ball fine. He just can't hit it often enough.

What makes him worth 38 projected home runs anyway is that when he does make contact, almost nothing hits it harder: 94.0 mph average exit velocity, 20.6% barrel rate, 58.8% hard-hit rate, all at the very top of the Statcast scale. That's the entire argument for the .358 OBP projection alongside a .227 average — pitchers can't afford to challenge him, so they don't, and his 17.2% walk rate reflects that negotiation. If the strikeout rate compresses even modestly as he continues adjusting to MLB sequencing, the .514 projected SLG becomes underselling him; if it doesn't, you have an all-or-nothing masher who needs the walk rate to stay elite just to remain an average regular.

report_llm.text: A 2.70 xERA with a 5.0% walk rate is the kind of combination that makes you stop scrolling. Henderson isn't missing bats at an elite clip — 28.1% whiff rate and a 31.9% chase rate are both middling — but he's strangling contact quality and refusing to give away free baserunners, and the xwOBA of .256 shows it's not smoke. The projection has him at 97.3 innings and a 3.10 ERA, which probably undersells what the Statcast profile is describing; the gap between his 93.0 mph fastball and a 94th-percentile xERA says the profile runs on shape and command, not heat, and the day that command slips is the day the modest whiff numbers start to matter. Right now he profiles as a legitimate mid-rotation piece who doesn't need strikeouts to get outs, which is a more durable thing than it sounds.

reports.name: Jefferson Rojas
reports.published_report: The contact-to-power ratio at AA is what makes this interesting. Jefferson Rojas is hitting .270 with a .196 ISO and 17 home runs through 453 plate appearances at AA, and his 16% strikeout rate translates to a 19.3% clip in MLB-equivalent terms, a figure most big-league hitters don't reach. The power reads as real enough for a 21-year-old corner profile, but the walk rate, 9% at AA, translating to 8.0%, is barely a tick shy of the MLB average, and the .336 OBP exposes the gap between his bat-to-ball ability and his willingness to take a free pass. If the contact stays and the walk rate doesn't grow, you're looking at a bench bat with some pop; if the discipline develops even modestly, the ceiling lifts toward a low-end everyday third baseman.

reports.name: Xavier Isaac
reports.published_report: The walk rate carries the argument here. Xavier Isaac has drawn 79 walks against 117 strikeouts across 416 PA at AA, and a 19% walk rate in Double-A that translates to 14.1% at the MLB level is the kind of discipline that plays anywhere. The ISO is also doing real work, .252 at AA with 23 home runs, and even after the level adjustment it lands at .178, well clear of the MLB translation average of .150. The problem is that the strikeout load translates to 29% when the MLB translation average sits at 22%, and at first base, with a ceiling the profile puts at bench or platoon bat, there isn't enough defensive value to carry a lineup spot through a bad month of contact. If the walk rates hold and he squeezes more contact out of that bat-to-ball profile, he's a genuine everyday option; if the strikeouts stay punishing and the BABIP normalizes below .321, you're looking at a left-handed bench piece with a good eye.

reports.name: Brandon Lowe
reports.published_report: The power is legitimate and the Statcast profile shows exactly why: 91.2 mph average exit velocity, a 12.2% barrel rate, and 46.8% hard-hit rate all cluster in the 80th percentile range, and the projection's 33 home runs in 658 plate appearances follows naturally from contact that consistently leaves the bat that hard. The catch is the 34.9% whiff rate, which sits at the 4th percentile, meaning his contact quality coexists with some of the worst swing-and-miss in baseball. That whiff rate is what keeps xBA at .241 and holds the xwOBA to .327, which is fine but not imposing, and it's the reason the .788 OPS projection feels right rather than conservative. If the strikeouts compress even modestly he's a genuine middle-of-the-order second baseman; if they don't, he's a 33-homer bat who bleeds enough at-bats that you're always negotiating his lineup spot.

reports.name: Roki Sasaki
reports.published_report: The stuff is legitimate — 97.9 mph on the fastball and a 29.7% whiff rate are genuinely loud numbers, but the current MLB profile shows a 9.3% walk rate that's eating every advantage they create. Hitters are making hard contact at a 43.9% clip and barreling him at 9.8%, which is why the xERA sits at 4.23 despite the movement and the chase numbers. A 33.1% chase rate should be punishing; it isn't yet, because the free passes keep the lineup turning over with fresh at-bats. The projection lands at a 4.37 ERA over 148.0 innings, which is a back-of-the-rotation contributor, not the ace the repertoire teases at, and the whole profile hinges on whether he can tighten the zone enough to let the whiff numbers do their actual work.

reports.name: Braylon Doughty
reports.published_report: The walk rate is doing most of the heavy lifting here. Across AA & A+, Doughty has issued just 20 walks in 89.4 innings, a 2.0 BB/9 that translates to 2.7 at the MLB level, comfortably below what most big-league starters allow. The strikeout stuff is more modest, a 10.7 K/9 that translates closer to the MLB mean, which means the profile lives or dies on that command staying this precise as opponents get better. If it holds, the 23% K-BB% across AA & A+ and a 3.3 ERA point toward a useful late reliever or multi-inning arm; if the walks tick up when he faces a sharper level of hitter, there isn't a swing-and-miss ceiling to bail him out.

reports.name: Emil Morales
reports.published_report: The bat is loud for a 19-year-old at this level, and the power is the argument: a .259 ISO across A+ & A ranks at the 95th percentile in his pool, with 24 home runs in 486 plate appearances. The .295/.382/.554 line looks like a future regular until you run the translation, where the 26% strikeout rate climbs to 29.7% in MLB equivalent terms against a league baseline of 22.0%. That gap is the whole profile in miniature — the pop translates (.163 ISO equivalent, barely above the MLB mean), the contact does not, and at shortstop against progressively better fastballs, 29.7% is a real ceiling discussion. If Morales tightens the zone and keeps the loft, there's a legitimate everyday profile here; if the strikeout rate is structural, you're looking at a bench bat with some thump.

reports.name: Kazuma Okamoto
reports.published_report: Thirty-two projected home runs is the easy part to explain; a 12.5% barrel rate does that kind of work. What's harder to square is a 33.6% whiff rate sitting alongside exit velocity and barrel numbers that would suggest a much cleaner hitter — the contact quality shows up in a .426 xSLG, but the bat misses often enough that a .217 xBA is where you land, and the .231 projected average reflects that honestly. Okamoto is the rare profile where the power translates without the batting average following it, and the .741 projected OPS lands well below what his raw thump implies because he's going to give back a lot of those runs at the plate. If the strikeout rate ever softens even modestly, there's a legitimate middle-of-the-order bat here; if it doesn't, you're looking at a 30-homer corner guy with a below-.303 OBP who needs every one of those barrels to carry his value.

reports.name: Troy Melton
reports.published_report: The Statcast contact profile is doing the heavy lifting: a 5.2% barrel rate and 34.9% hard-hit rate both sitting in strong territory, which is why his xwOBA of .272 and xERA of 3.06 land at the 87th percentile despite a strikeout rate of 22.2%, right around the middle of the league. He gets there by chasing hitters off the zone, a 32.9% chase rate, and keeping the ball off barrels rather than missing bats. The 2.29 ERA and 1.07 WHIP in the projection read as optimistic given the 25.9% whiff rate offers almost no insurance if command slides, and the whole profile hinges on staying near that 7.6% walk rate, because a tick upward and the soft contact stops carrying him. At 96.4 mph with that shape, he's a mid-rotation contributor if the zone command holds and a swingman with a flattering ERA in a short sample if it doesn't.

reports.name: Javier Sanoja
reports.published_report: An 8.3% strikeout rate is almost unheard of in today's game, and that's the whole bet on Sanoja. The problem is the rest of the contact profile: 86.5 mph average exit velocity and a 2.3% barrel rate that sits in the bottom tier of the league, which is why his xwOBA clocks at .278 despite all that contact. He makes enough contact to run a useful batting average, and 28.7 ft/s gives him genuine baserunning value, but the projection's .419 SLG hinges entirely on whether his bat-to-ball skill can coax something more from weak contact than it currently does. If the power doesn't develop, you're looking at a slap-contact bench piece who's useful in the right lineup spot and a problem anywhere else.

reports.name: Adrian Morejon
reports.published_report:
A 2.3% barrel rate, a 37.6% chase rate, a 99.3 mph fastball. The Statcast profile here isn't even close.

Morejon's xERA sits at 2.46 and his xwOBA at .244, both at the 97th percentile, and the chase rate slots at the 98th, which tells you contact isn't happening because hitters aren't making good decisions against him, not because they're getting lucky. The 34.4% whiff rate pairs with a walk rate of 6.8%, which is the only legitimate lever to watch: if the command slips, the profile softens from elite to merely very good. ValuCast projects a 2.82 ERA over 82.1 innings out of the San Diego bullpen, and given what the batted-ball numbers look like, that may still leave room on the table.

reports.name: José Ramírez
reports.published_report: The .284 xBA sits at the 93rd percentile, the walk rate matches it there, and the strikeout rate comes in at 12.4% — contact and discipline that almost never travel together at that level. What's missing is the barrel rate: 5.0% puts him at the 25th percentile, which is why the projection lands at 16 home runs across 554 PA rather than the kind of power he was posting in his prime. The speed (37 projected steals) and the plate discipline carry the profile now, and the .343 OBP holds up even as the power thins, so what's left if the exit velocity doesn't improve is a high-OBP, high-SB second-division regular who still grades well in the field. Not a disaster, just a different player than Cleveland built around.

reports.name: Bryan Reynolds
reports.published_report: The tension in Reynolds's profile is the gap between how hard he hits the ball and how often he misses it. His 13.4% walk rate sits in elite territory, and his 46.8% hard-hit rate translates to a .348 xwOBA that suggests a better hitter than his raw numbers have recently advertised, but a 28.9% whiff rate undercuts the contact quality, explaining why the xBA lands at .247 even as the power and patience numbers scream above-average. The profile resolves into a patient, pull-side thumper who takes his walks, runs into 19 home runs across a full season, and carries enough OBP (.363 projected) to profile as a solid everyday outfielder rather than a star. The ceiling stays capped at this level as long as the whiff rate stays where it is.

The problem is the 11.4% walk rate, which is where the profile gets honest about its limits, because a reliever throwing 100.5 mph with a 29.6% whiff rate and a 34.0% chase rate who also walks more than one in nine batters is leaving leverage on the table every time command slips. reports.name: Steven Kwan

reports.name: Orion Kerkering
reports.published_report: The contact-suppression numbers are the headline: an average exit velocity of 85.0 mph and a hard-hit rate of 29.1% that both sit at the very top of the relief leaderboard, and the 3.13 xERA shows what that does to expected run prevention. Kerkering doesn't miss bats at an elite clip, 24.8% strikeouts and a 26.7% whiff rate are solid but not the engine here, the engine is that when hitters make contact, it's weak. The walk rate, 11.9%, is the one number that keeps this from being a setup-closer argument, and the 3.62 projected ERA against that 3.13 xERA tells you the walks are costing him real runs. If the command firms up even modestly, the profile becomes one of the more legitimate setup arms in the NL East; if it doesn't, he's exactly what the 18 projected holds say: useful, sometimes dominant in the zone, and leaking runs the inning he loses the plate.

reports.name: Brandon Sproat
reports.published_report: The fastball at 96.7 mph is the one thing working in Sproat's favor, and the Statcast profile makes clear how much is riding on it. His chase rate sits at 25.5%, which is about as low as it gets, and when hitters aren't chasing, an 11.6% walk rate is what you get. The strikeout rate at 24.2% is league-average territory, not bad, but his xERA of 4.85 and a hard-hit rate of 43.1% say he's not missing barrels consistently enough to survive contact. reports.name: Matt McLain

The barrel rate at 10.4% is real enough to support the 16 projected home runs across a full season, and 19 stolen bases from a 28.6 ft/s sprint speed is the kind of secondary value that keeps him relevant in a mixed lineup, but the whole offensive profile hinges on whether the whiff rate comes down — at 28.1%, he's leaving walks on the table that his chase discipline earns him. Either the strikeout rate softens and he becomes a useful table-setter with sneaky pop, or it doesn't, and .205 with an .OPS at .662 is exactly what you get.

reports.name: Jaison Chourio
reports.published_report: Thirty-two stolen bases across AA & A+ at 21 years old is the loudest number in this profile, and the plate discipline underneath it is what keeps this from being a speed-only conversation. His 14% walk rate across AA & A+ translates to 11.2% at the MLB level, and MLB hitters average 8.5%, meaning Chourio can reach base without needing to hit; a .373 OBP on a .268 average tells that story cleanly. The power is the honest ceiling check: his .145 ISO across AA & A+ translates to just .12 at the MLB level, and when most big-league hitters are sitting at .15, that gap matters for how you use him. If the speed and on-base hold and the power stays where it is, he's a solid everyday center fielder who beats opponents a different way; if the power never arrives and the hit tool plateaus, he slides toward a second-division regular who presses when the bases are empty.

reports.name: Francisco Lindor
reports.published_report: The contact numbers lie. Lindor's xwOBA sits at .349 and his hard-hit rate at 48.4%, yet his actual average has been running well below what a .252 xBA implies — the gap between what he earns on contact and what he's gotten back is the whole tension in this profile. The projection's .243 AVG reflects that leakage, not a hitter who has lost his ability to do damage. What keeps the ceiling capped is legs that have cooled to the 31st percentile in sprint speed, which limits both the stolen-base utility and his margin for error on balls in play, and the 11.0% walk rate has to keep doing the heavy lifting on OBP if the batting average doesn't normalize. If contact luck evens out even modestly, the .764 OPS projection looks conservative; if it doesn't, you're carrying a shortstop with good underlying power who can't quite get the hits to show up.

reports.name: Spencer Miles
reports.published_report: The xERA of 2.99 and a barrel rate of 3.5% tell you what's actually happening when Miles faces hitters: they're making contact, but almost none of it is doing damage. That's the whole profile. He doesn't miss many bats, a 18.7% whiff rate is bottom-of-the-barrel stuff, but his walk rate is tidy at 6.2% and batters can't get under balls against him, which keeps the xwOBA at .269 and the average exit velo at 86.7 mph. The 94.4 projected innings with zero quality starts says Toronto is using him in a hybrid shape, which is probably the right call for a pitcher whose value lives in contact suppression rather than swing-and-miss, and if he ever draws a longer leash and the barrel suppression slips even modestly, the lack of a strikeout ceiling becomes a real problem.

reports.name: Mookie Betts
reports.published_report: The contact grades are elite and the power is fading. Betts's 11.5% strikeout rate and 19.7% chase rate sit at the very top of the league, meaning he still puts the barrel on almost anything near the zone, but a 38.3% hard-hit rate and a .430 xSLG tell you the pop behind that contact has softened considerably. The projection (.245/.305/.424 across 518 PA) lands him as a league-average or slightly below offensive player, which would have been unthinkable five years ago, and the 6.8% walk rate suggests the plate discipline isn't fully converting into on-base value the way it once did. If the exit velocity holds and the hard-hit rate climbs back, there's a .270-plus hitter with real pop still in here; if this is the new normal, you're looking at a second-division regular carrying his value mostly through contact rate, fielding, and name.

reports.name: Yamal Encarnacion

Forty-eight at AA across 395 plate appearances is a legitimate weapon, and the 18 K% at that level translates to 21.3% in the majors, right at the 22.0% MLB average, meaning the contact ability that makes the speed playable should survive the climb. The power doesn't travel: a .117 ISO at AA becomes .11 in an MLB context, and the average sits at .15. He has drawn 24 walks against those same 25 strikeouts, and that contact-and-patience combination at catcher is what the profile lives on, because the power is not going to carry anyone: the .131 ISO at AAA translates to .126 MLB-equivalent, light for the position. If the contact rate holds, he becomes a bench or platoon catcher with a real reason to be on a roster; if major-league velocity flattens it, what remains is a depth receiver without enough bat to matter.

The control grades out fine, but if the contact suppression keeping that WHIP pristine doesn't survive the climb, the strikeout rate isn't a safety net. The ceiling here is a depth arm, the floor is a depth arm, and the honest gap between them is how many levels that WHIP holds before something gives.

reports.name: Ubaldo Soto
reports.published_report: The 104 strikeouts are loud. Across 79.7 innings at A-ball, Ubaldo Soto is missing bats at 11.8 K/9, which translates to just under the MLB average at the big-league level, while his 5.1 BB/9 translates to a walk rate that dwarfs what big-league pitching typically allows. The K-BB% sits at the 70th percentile among A-ball arms, which is the one number holding the profile together, and the whole thing hinges on whether the command ever closes that gap: if it doesn't, you have a depth arm who racks up strikeouts in the minors and racks up walks everywhere else.

reports.name: Carlos Duran
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is loud, 12.6 K/9 at AAA translating to 9.8 at the MLB level while the MLB mean sits at 8.6, but 29 walks in 45.7 innings is the whole argument against him. That walk burden translates to a 4.6 BB/9 in MLB terms, nearly a run and a half above the 3.2 MLB mean, and once you net strikeouts against walks the K-BB% lands exactly at the MLB average of 13.5%. The swing stuff earns him a look; command is the specific dependency, and if it stays where it is, the strikeouts stop being an asset and start being damage control. Either a usable depth arm if the walks come down, or organizational filler if they don't.

reports.name: Wilson Rodriguez
reports.published_report: The walk rate is loud for a 21-year-old at A+: 58 walks across 364 plate appearances, with a translated BB% of 11.4 against a big-league pool that averages 8.5. That's the selling point. The power doesn't come with it — an ISO of .167 at A+ translates to .127 in the majors, meaningfully short of the 8.5 average, and the 20 stolen bases show he knows he has to manufacture something when he does get on. If the plate discipline holds as he climbs and the raw pop develops enough to punish pitchers for nibbling, there's a fringe regular in here; if the power stays where it is, he's a bench piece with a useful OBP, and the ceiling note in the data says the system agrees.

If he sharpens the command, he's a back-end depth arm; if he doesn't, the floor is exactly where the ceiling is.
